title: The Numbers in the Coins
sub: Grades 5–8 · Math · Timelines, ratios and the widow’s gift
objective: Students will use the numbers on the eleven coins of *In Their Hands* to find spans of years on a BC/AD timeline, using the rule that there is no year zero; place dates on a number line, using negative numbers as a model; compare measured coins in grams and millimeters; work with the ratio of a half-shekel to a shekel; and explain, as a fraction of all she had, why Jesus said the widow’s two small coins were more than all the others gave.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every date and amount on a coin is a number with a meaning. Reading it right means remembering there is no year zero, and asking what a number is a share of.

items.text: find the span of years between two dates: both AD, both BC, or across the join
items.question: find a span of years, even across BC and AD?

items.text: explain why there is no year zero, and why a span from *b* BC to *a* AD is *a* + *b* − 1 years
items.question: explain why you take away one across the join?

items.text: use a ratio and a percent to explain why the widow’s two small coins were more than all the others gave
items.question: use a percent to explain the widow’s gift?

items.text: prove the no-year-zero rule with algebra
items.question: prove the no-year-zero rule with algebra?

materials: A strip of tape on the board for a class timeline; centimeter rulers (Red level)
The Pilate prutah card on the handouts, or the coin on the exhibition page
Differentiated handouts, one per student; the answer key is page 3
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** the Gospel Timeline walks the eleven coins in date order, from the census under Augustus to Paul’s appeal before Festus; students can check each span as they go. In Case 7, find the widow’s two lepta and Pilate’s prutah, 1.79 g and 16 mm.

steps.title: What year came before AD 1?
script: Ask: *“If this is AD 1, what year came just before it?”* Most students say *year zero*.

line.alt: A number line of years: AD 1, AD 2 and AD 3 on the right. The year just before AD 1 is a question mark.

steps.purpose: Bring out the year-zero mistake before the rule is taught.
students: If this is AD 1, what year came just before it?

steps.title: No year zero
script: Draw the line below and tell them there was none: the years are counted from one, so 1 BC is followed straight away by AD 1. Then ask how long the Shekel of Tyre’s dates, 1 BC to AD 1, really span. One year — not two.

line.alt: A number line from 3 BC to AD 3. 1 BC is followed straight away by AD 1: there is no year zero between them.

steps.purpose: Fix the fact the whole lesson rests on: 1 BC is followed straight away by AD 1.
students: The Shekel of Tyre (a replica) is dated 1 BC–AD 1. How many years is that?

steps.title: Both AD, or both BC
script: **Both dates AD.** Subtract as usual. Claudius reigned from AD 41 to 54: 54 − 41 = 13 years.
**Both dates BC.** BC numbers count *down* toward the join, so the earlier date is the bigger number. Herod the Great ruled from 37 BC until his death in 4 BC: 37 − 4 = 33 years.

examples.title: Both dates AD
examples.alt: A bronze coin of the emperor Claudius: his head
steps: Both dates are AD, so subtract as usual: **54 − 41**.

examples.title: Both dates BC
examples.alt: Herod the Great’s bronze prutah: symbols and no human image
steps: Herod the Great ruled from **37 BC** until his death in **4 BC**.
BC numbers count *down* toward the join, so the earlier date is the bigger number.

steps.purpose: Practice the two simpler spans, and see why BC numbers count down.
students: Why is the earlier BC date the bigger number?
Try Pilate, prefect from AD 26 to AD 36.

steps.title: Across the join
script: **Across the join.** Add, then take away one, because there is no year zero: hop from 2 BC to AD 2 and count three hops, not four. Work Augustus together (below).

**The model and its flaw.** Treat BC years as negative numbers: 27 BC sits at −27, AD 14 at +14. The distance from −27 to 14 is 41: one too many, because a number line has a zero and the calendar does not.

line.alt: A number line from 3 BC to AD 3, with no year zero between 1 BC and AD 1. Three hops run from 2 BC to AD 2: to 1 BC, to AD 1, to AD 2.

worked.title: How long did Augustus rule?
worked.alt: A bronze coin of Augustus: the emperor’s head
steps: Augustus ruled from **27 BC** until his death in **AD 14**.
Count back from 27 BC to the join: 27 years. Count on from the join to AD 14: 14 years. **27 + 14 = 41.**
The dates cross from BC to AD, and there is no year zero to stand on, so take away one: **41 − 1 = 40 years.**

screen.rule:
From *b* BC to *a* AD is *a* + *b* − 1 years.
From 2 BC to AD 2: 2 + 2 − 1 = **3**.

steps.purpose: Learn the rule for crossing from BC to AD, and why it takes away one.
students: Count the hops from 2 BC to AD 2. Does the rule agree?
On a number line, −27 to 14 is 41. Why is that one too many?

steps.title: Half a shekel, all she had
script: **Two more strands.** Every Jewish man over twenty owed a half-shekel Temple tax each year: a ratio of 1 : 2, so in Matthew 17:27 one coin worth a shekel pays for Jesus and Peter. And the widow gave two lepta, *everything* she had: 2 out of 2 is 100%.

examples.title: The Temple tax
examples.alt: The Shekel of Tyre, a silver coin. A museum-quality replica
steps: Every Jewish man over twenty owed a **half-shekel** Temple tax each year.
In Matthew 17:27, one coin worth a shekel pays for two people: Jesus and Peter.

examples.title: The widow’s gift
examples.alt: One of the widow’s two lepta: a small, worn bronze coin
steps: She gave two lepta: *everything* she had.

steps.purpose: Meet the other two strands of the handouts: a ratio and a percent.
students: How many shekels pay the Temple tax for 6 men?
*Invented numbers:* someone has 100 coins and gives 10. What percent is that?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three use the same coins and dates.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: A worked example, then guided spans: AD dates, BC dates, and dates across the join. Place five coins on a number line. Find the widow’s gift as a fraction and a percent, and the Temple tax for a group of men.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Mixed problems: the no-year-zero rule, a table of six spans to rank, Pilate’s coin and the regnal year of Tiberius, the two measured coins, thirty shekels and the Temple tax, and three givers compared by amount and by percent.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Prove the no-year-zero rule with algebra, solve multi-step date problems, build a timeline to scale from 103 BC to AD 62, and use an equation to compare the widow’s gift with a large gift that is a small fraction of great wealth.

steps.purpose: Practice the rules independently at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the same coins and dates.

steps.title: Exit ticket
script: *1. How many years from 4 BC to AD 39, the dates on the coin of Herod Antipas?* (42.) *2. The widow gave the least money. In what mathematical sense did she give the most?* (The largest share of what she had: 100%.)
